On Thursday, December 8, 2011 9:17:06 AM UTC-5, Richard Chandler wrote:
Hi Patrick,

Here is a leave-one-site-out cross-validation example that I had laying around. Use with caution! There are no safety checks and this will give you misleading results if you compare models fitted to data with different numbers of missing values. Note also that there are many other, possibly better, ways of doing this type of thing.

Richard

library(unmarked)
set.seed(33140)
example(unmarked) # Fits 3 occupancy models fm1,fm2,fm3

# Discrepancy measures
cost.fn1 <- function(observed, expected) mean(abs(observed-expected)>0.5)
cost.fn2 <- function(observed, expected) sum((observed-expected)^2)

xval <- function(fm, cost) {
   umf <- getData(fm)
   nSites <- numSites(umf)
   cv <- 0
   for(i in 1:nSites) {
       test <- umf[i,] # leave one site out
       train <- umf[-i,]
       fmu <- update(fm, data=train)
       E.psi <- predict(fmu, type="state", newdata=test)[,1]
       E.p <- predict(fmu, type="det", newdata=test)[,1]
       E <- E.psi * E.p
       y <- as.vector(getY(test))
       cv <- cv + cost(y, E)
   }
   return(cv)
}

xval(fm1, cost=cost.fn2)
xval(fm2, cost=cost.fn2)
xval(fm3, cost=cost.fn2) # Lowest error

messages.body_plain:
Hi BK,

Thank you for clearly articulating your question.

In this model, lambda is the expected number of individuals in year 1. Abundance after year 1 is modeled as the sum of 2 random variables (recruits and survivors). So if you want to model abundance throughout time, you need to model lambda as a function of corn in year 1, and gamma and/or omega as a function of corn. In other words, in addition to supplying corn as a yearlySiteCov, you need to create a siteCov that has the corn data from the first year:

veg.umf <- unmarkedFramePCO(..., siteCovs = data.frame(corn1 = habitat$Corn.1))
fm1 <- pcountOpen(~corn1, ~corn, ~1, ~1, veg.umf) # note the two names corn1 and corn

HTH,

Richard

yea you could do that if N[j] = number of species at a location "j"

the problem with this approach is that (1) the model doesn't preserve species identity across sample units and thus you cannot model species-level effects (the whole point of the Dorazio-Royle papers).
(2) related: you cannot model "heterogeneity" in encounter probability because unmarked does not handle model Mh in that context.

I actually think (2) would be easy to resolve if someone had a half-day to spend on it.....

Also, you can estimate species richness in unmarked using an occupancy model as is described in the Occupancy book.  You need to have a list of all possible species in the study area.

For a multiple-species model, what for me, is different than a species richnes model, I did (2 species as the most simple example):

The example is using occupancy

Data: mult  (I especified Species as a site covariate), You need to put all your sites repeated as many as the number of species that you want to model.

Site  DH       Species

1      101          A
2       000         A
3       111         A
4       010         A
1      111          B
2      000          B
3      010          B
4      101          B

mod1 <- occu(~ Species ~ Species , mult)
mod2 <- occu(~ 1 ~ Species , mult)

In the mod1 I am asking for a detection probability different for each species and occupancy also different for each species.  May be I am wrong but that is what I did.

In mod2, detection probability is equal for the 2 species.  You can try other models.

Best,

Manuel

messages.body_plain:
You should check out the methods of this paper.  It offers a method to model how the presence of Species A affects the occurrence of Species B when both are detected imperfectly.  It only works one way, so you have to assume that one species is dominant and is unaffected by the presence of the other.  This can be done easily in WinBUGS.

Waddle, J. H., R. M. Dorazio, S. C. Walls, K. G. Rice, J. Beauchamp, M. J. Schuman, and F. J. Mazzotti. 2010. A new parameterization for estimating co-occurrence of interacting species. Ecological Applications 20:1467-1475.

messages.subject: Re: Multi-species models
messages.body_plain:
The difference between the multi-species community model (to which
Richard Chandler is referring) and the DeWan et al (2009) approach is
the treatment of species as fixed or random effects.

DeWan et al (2009) used species as a fixed effect, and assumed that
the functional response to covariates was the same across species.
For instance, one of their models was psi(species + p/a).  The
estimate of the fixed effect for perimeter/area ratio (p/a) was
potentially improved (i.e., greater precision) because it used the
response data from all the species combined.  But this forced the
fixed effect for p/a to be the same for each species, albeit, with
species-specific intercepts.  Now if they had included a species*p/a
interaction, then their model would no longer be pooling species
response data for the functional relationship of p/a and the results
would be the same as running separate regressions for each species.
In which case, there is no "improvement" in the modeling effort.

Using species as a random effect in a true multi-species community
model comes with it's own restrictions/assumptions, but it represents
a more flexible framework for modeling multiple species.  This assumes
you have more than ~10 species, otherwise the random effects
distribution (or the prior) will not be adequately estimated.  Like
Richard said, I'm trying to build on some code that Richard and Andy
(and Ian) have started to allow a multi-species model to be estimated
using maximum likelihood in unmarked.  It is tricky though...

-----------------------

different habitat covariates using function pcountOpen. We have point
count data for different species and some of the species are highly
abundant (more than 3000 at one point count survey). This compelled us
to set high value for K and the run time is unbearably slow. We tried
with se=FALSE and different starting values but there were not much
improvement in run time. There is no way that we can do our modeling
at this speed (>3 days to run a model). As you said in an earlier
thread, the main problem is the high value of K.

In fact, we are not interested in the abundance estimate but in its
relationship with the habitat covariates. We are trying to investigate
the influence of habitat covariate upon the species abundance.  In
such case, can we divide all the count data by some arbitrary number
like 10 or 100 (so that we can use a significantly lower number for K)
and run the model to look at the effect of habitat covariates on
abundance?
Thanks

There are two easily mangeable data formats for using  in unmarked:

1. observation level distance data
   a matrix with n individuals rows and 2 columns:  [distance, sample unit ID]

2. Multinomial frequencies:  A matrix of nsites x (n distance classes)  where element [i,j] is the number of individuals counted at point i and distance class j.

It sounds like you have type 1.  I think the following example is in the help file or perhaps the vignette PDF that comes with unmarked:

> library(unmarked)
> dists <- read.csv(system.file("csv", "distdata.csv", package="unmarked"))
> head(dists, 10)
distance transect

2 18 a
3 7  a
4 2  a
5 13 b
...

> levels(dists$transect)

I was intending to use pcount to estimate relative abundance of
invasive Brown Treesnakes from multiple sites on Guam (Andy, I'm sure
you'll recall working with my colleague Amy Yackel Adams).

We visit each site multiple (many, many) times.  The few snakes we
find are removed.  Our detection rates are so low with respect to our
expectations of snake density, and surveys occur over extended periods
of time, so I was willing to make the assumption that our removals did
not influence N in any meaningful way.

I've just come across the multinomPois option with type="removal"...it
seems I should be using this, right?  However, we have as many as 500
searches at a single site (the vast majority resulting in no snake
observations)...can this function "handle" a multinomial with 500 cell
probabilities?

Shane Siers

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Predicting p
messages.body_plain:
Hi Aude,

1) Selection of a "best model" model is often very subjective, even using AIC. Usually models are thrown out if parameters don't converge, if additional parameters don't seem to be adding things etc. If your "AIC best model" is getting a lot of weight and the parameters converge you'd at least have some justification to use it. Just be aware that and AIC table isn't as cut and dry of a model selection criteria as is often advertised. If there is a lot of ambiguity, may want to model average (see examples at the bottom of ?fitList) .
2) If you look at detection1, it should have 4 rows. Predict will generate a prediction for each unique row of covariates
3) For detection2, it looks like visit has length 4, but hour has length of 942, under a data.frame, this won't do. What exactly are you trying to do?
4) I am running a suite of 257 models (bad, I know), but the modSel and prediction on this suite can take a very, very long time (well more than an hour, on a fairly high end machine).

Matthew

messages.subject: large parameter estimates using 'occu'
messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

I'm performing a simple single season occupancy model, with response variable as presence/absence.  All state (site) covariates (10) are continuous, while my observation covariates are both continuous and categorical.  While my global model produces parameter estimates in the range of +-5, most nested models generate parameter estimates in the 10's to 100's, even with the detection probs modeled with intercept only, which prevents interpretation of the odds ratios and effect sizes.

Using the standard glm function (excluding and including observation covariates) in R results in parameter estimates typically seen in logistic regression with values ranging around +/- 1.

I know models that use categorical variables only can suffer from this situation if one of the categories is not represented in either of the response outcomes, but this is not the case with my continuous variables.

Has anyone experienced a similar situation, and if so do you have suggestions for a remedy?

Thanks
Patrick

Hi Aude,

In general, if there is nothing weird with your AIC best model (that is, all parameters were estimable, no parameters have infinite variance), the decision to use a model with deltaAIC>20 is very defensible, especially within the wildlife community. In general, the IC folk kind of frown on p-value approaches.
